article_text:
LYON, France — When Mexican costume designer Anna Terrazas told Todd Haynes that the most important thing about a costume was what it smelled like, the filmmaker had just one response: “You’re hired.”

The Oscar-nominated director shared the anecdote about his upcoming Pedro Pascal-starring romantic noir drama “De Noche” at the Lumière Film Festival on Tuesday, offering a glimpse into his approach to filmmaking, from the music and sounds that shape his movies to the senses that cannot always be expressed on screen.

'Nobody Wants This' Creator Erin Foster on Adam Brody's Support for Palestine: 'I Disagree With Him, and That's OK'

“We see movies with our ears and our eyes,” Haynes explained. “But movies that evoke smell and touch and other kinds of senses are the ones that keep allowing us to fill in.”

Popular on Variety

Haynes is in Lyon with longtime producer Christine Vachon for a retrospective featuring four of his films: “Poison,” “Safe,” “Far From Heaven” and “I’m Not There,” including newly restored versions of the first two.

The director – whose latest film follows the story of a detective (Pascal) and a younger schoolteacher (Danny Ramirez) who flee the corruption of 1930s Los Angeles for Mexico – described the homework he sets himself before each production. He said he immerses himself in films that share its genre or cinematic style, rather than necessarily its historical setting.

“It’s as if I give myself an assignment each time,” he said, explaining how that research feeds into what he calls his “image books,” which he shares with his collaborators.

While putting together the image book for his Oscar-nominated “May December,” starring frequent collaborator Julianne Moore alongside Natalie Portman, Haynes began listening to Michel Legrand ‘s score for Joseph Losey’s “The Go-Between.”

The music soon became central to the project. He played it on set from the very first day, using it to choreograph camera movements. By the editing stage, the music had become so integral to the film that Haynes asked composer Marcelo Zarvos to rearrange and adapt it. “We couldn’t let it go,” he recalled. “It became a definitive part of the structure, the language, and the energy of the film.”

Having watched the restored version of “Safe” the previous evening in Lyon, Haynes praised sound designer Leslie Shatz for the unsettling soundscape of the 1995 drama, in which Moore plays a woman suffering from a mysterious illness.

He described “all of the strange, lurking, unconscious sounds” in the film, that created what he called “a kind of magnetic field in which the contamination she senses from her surroundings becomes literally audible.”

Turning to his six-time Oscar-nominated 2015 romance “Carol,” Haynes recalled how journalists kept congratulating him and stars Cate Blanchett and Cannes Best Actress winner Rooney Mara for portraying strong women. Blanchett, he said, would object: Carol wasn’t some invincible heroine but a woman constrained by her time, struggling to understand herself and how she wanted to live.

“There is something radical and anti-social about love,” Haynes said, citing great French writer Roland Barthes’ “A Lover’s Discourse,” passages of which he shared with the actors.

Haynes also paid tribute to Vachon, who helped rescue “Safe” when he was struggling to raise its $1 million budget. The film, he said, wouldn’t exist without her.

Vachon, who already had a grasp of the industry’s commercial realities, recalled the practical advice she gave him years earlier when he proposed making his first feature, “Poison” as three interconnected 20-minute stories.

“I said, you know what, Todd? Make it 90 minutes,” she recalled.

The producer made some pointed observations about the state of independent cinema. She sees younger Americans flocking to repertory theaters, including her own 26-year-old daughter, but worries about what the industry is offering them.

“I feel like we are creating a new generation of cinemagoers, but we’re just not giving them enough movies to see,” she said.

Haynes also revisited his childhood obsession with Lucille Ball, which inspired his autobiographical short “Dottie Gets Spanked.” He went on to tease a possible screening of the film alongside “Superstar: The Karen Carpenter Story,” his cult short made with Barbie dolls that has rarely been shown publicly since legal disputes over its music rights. The filmmaker was hinting heavily at what might be in store for the festival’s surprise screening Wednesday evening at the Institut Lumière.

The Lumière Film Festival runs in Lyon through Oct. 18.

title_original: Best of the Best review – college comedy formula gets a Bollywood makeover
editorial_title_zh: 《Best of the Best》评论：大学喜剧公式换上宝莱坞外衣
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这部讲述两位闺蜜与一场舞蹈比赛的影片，吸引人的并非熟悉的情节，而是快节奏的叙事与出色的编舞。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部 Netflix 喜剧讲述美国校园里宝莱坞舞蹈社团之间的竞争，情节毫无意外可言。每个转折都一目了然，每个角色都似曾相识，基本公式与十几部此前的大学喜剧如出一辙。但它风趣、节奏明快，并由 Lena Khan 以充沛的活力执导。Lena Khan 是为数不多在好莱坞工作的穆斯林女性电影人之一。编剧是 Hasan Minhaj 与 Prashanth Venkataramanujam，两位千禧一代喜剧演员，他们对 Z 世代行为的研究之深，几乎可以写一篇博士论文。", "links": [{"text": "Bollywood", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/bollywood"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Maya（Maitreyi Ramakrishnan 饰）与 Anjali（Priyanka Kedia 饰）是从小一起长大的密友，一同考入加州大学洛杉矶分校（UCLA）。Maya 聪明但难以相处，Anjali 则温柔漂亮。（不用说，Maya 也绝对是个大美人。）新生周，她们加入了校内的宝莱坞舞蹈社，Maya 很快就与社长 Ronak（Ankur Rathee 饰）在编舞上针锋相对。他想以宝莱坞婚礼为新一季的舞码主题，Maya 指出这未免有些老派。如果想击败对手，他们需要一些现代而新鲜的东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "结局不难猜。但这部喜剧节奏极快，还有大量“第二代移民”式的笑点。当 Anjali 的妈妈在宿舍楼的所有人面前扇了她一巴掌时，Maya 开玩笑说，那些白人孩子看起来像是想报警。影片结尾极为精彩：编舞的情节围绕一场对 Koh-i-Noor 钻石的盗窃展开，这颗钻石如今镶嵌在王冠之上。这段表演既表达了年轻、面向未来的南亚裔及其海外社群的态度，也庆祝了传统舞蹈。这一高潮会让你觉得，它稳居同类作品的顶峰。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "电影", "links": [{"text": "Film", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/film"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "喜剧电影", "links": [{"text": "Comedy films", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/comedy"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "宝莱坞", "links": [{"text": "Bollywood", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/bollywood"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "舞蹈", "links": [{"text": "Dance", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/dance"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "歌舞片", "links": [{"text": "Musicals", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/musical"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "喜剧", "links": [{"text": "Comedy", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/comedy"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "评论", "links": [{"text": "reviews", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tone/reviews"}], "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "T here is absolutely nothing unexpected about this Netflix comedy set in the world of rival Bollywood dance groups on American campuses. Each plot twist is instantly familiar, every character recognisable, the essential formula untweaked from a dozen previous college comedies. But it’s funny and snappy, and directed with infectious energy by Lena Khan, one of the few Muslim female film-makers working in Hollywood. The scriptwriters are Hasan Minhaj and Prashanth Venkataramanujam, a pair of millennial comedians who look as if they’ve done enough research on the inner workings of gen Z behaviour to write a PhD.", "links": [{"text": "Bollywood", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/bollywood"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Maya (Maitreyi Ramakrishnan) and Anjali (Priyanka Kedia) star as lifelong best friends who enrol together at UCLA. Maya is the clever difficult one; Anjali is the nice pretty one. (It goes without saying Maya is also a total babe.) article_text:
T here is absolutely nothing unexpected about this Netflix comedy set in the world of rival Bollywood dance groups on American campuses. Each plot twist is instantly familiar, every character recognisable, the essential formula untweaked from a dozen previous college comedies. But it’s funny and snappy, and directed with infectious energy by Lena Khan, one of the few Muslim female film-makers working in Hollywood. The scriptwriters are Hasan Minhaj and Prashanth Venkataramanujam, a pair of millennial comedians who look as if they’ve done enough research on the inner workings of gen Z behaviour to write a PhD.

Maya (Maitreyi Ramakrishnan) and Anjali (Priyanka Kedia) star as lifelong best friends who enrol together at UCLA. Maya is the clever difficult one; Anjali is the nice pretty one. (It goes without saying Maya is also a total babe.) During freshers’ week they join the college’s Bollywood dance club where, predictably, Maya locks horns with leader Ronak (Ankur Rathee) over the choreography. He wants to base their new-season routine on Bollywood weddings, which, as Maya points out, is a bit trad. If they are going to beat their rivals they will need to come up with something modern and fresh.

No prizes for guessing where this is headed. But the comedy is whip-fast, with plenty of second-generation in jokes. When Anjali’s mum slaps her in full view of the dorm house, Maya jokes that the white kids looked like they wanted to call the police. And it ends brilliantly with a choreography that has a plotline involving a heist of the Koh-i-Noor – the diamond now in the crown jewels. The sequence manages to say something about young future-facing south Asians and diaspora communities while also including a celebration of traditional dance. It’s a high note that will leave you thinking this is up there with the best.

article_text:
エルメス財団と東京藝術大学が「金属」をテーマに特別プログラムを開催。大巻伸嗣らが講師に

エルメス 財団と 東京藝術大学 が共催する「スキル・アカデミー」の冬の特別プログラムが、12月5日、6日、8日に開催される。金属加工の伝統技術を学ぶワークショップと、日仏の専門家によるラウンドテーブルを通じて、素材と人間の創造的な関係を探る。参加者の募集は11月11日まで。

エルメス 財団と 東京藝術大学 が共催する「スキル・アカデミー」の冬の特別プログラム「金属というトランスフォーメーション」が、2026年12月5日、6日、8日に東京藝術大学 上野キャンパスで開催される。

スキル・アカデミーは、2014年にフランス・パリでローンチされた、職人技術の継承と未来に向けた革新の両立を目指す教育・研究プログラム。素材やものづくりの技術に目を向け、その知識や実践を共有するさまざまなの機会を提供しており、今回の特別プログラムは、2025年から2026年にかけて取り組んできた「金属」というテーマの締めくくりに位置づけられる。

12月5日と6日に開催されるワークショップでは、東京藝術大学の工房を舞台に、彫金、鍛金、鋳金という3つの金属加工技術を学ぶ。金属を叩き、成形し、彫るといった身体的な作業を通じて、素材の性質や加工技術への理解を深めるとともに、スプーンなどの制作にも取り組む。

講師を務めるのは、東京藝術大学工芸科教授で彫金作家の前田宏智、同教授で鍛金作家の丸山智巳、同准教授で鋳金作家の三枝一将と佐治真理子。さらに、彫刻科教授で現代美術家の 大巻伸嗣 も参加する。

金属は古くから道具や 建築 、装飾、彫刻など、さまざまな領域で用いられてきた素材だ。今回のワークショップでは、そうした金属と人間の暮らしとの関係を見つめ直すとともに、素材に直接触れ、加工するという行為そのものに焦点を当てる。

工芸技術を単なる制作手段として捉えるのではなく、素材との対話を通じて新たな表現の可能性を探る点も、このプログラムの特徴だ。伝統的な金属加工の技法と現代美術の実践が交差することで、ものづくりにおける身体性や技術の継承について考える機会となりそうだ。

また、12月8日には、日本とフランスの専門家をオンラインでつなぐラウンドテーブルを開催。金属をテーマに活動してきた2年間の集大成として、金属のものづくりや技術、表現について国境を越えた対話を行う。登壇者やプログラムの詳細は後日発表される。

ワークショップの対象は、16歳以上の創作活動を専門とする人、20歳以上の教育従事者、12〜15歳のプログラムに関心のある人のいずれかに該当する人で、定員は約15人。参加費は無料で、応募多数の場合は抽選となる。応募期間は10月19日から11月11日まで。銀座メゾンエルメスのウェブサイトから申し込むことができる。

article_text:
Source: Lea Meienberg / Philip Leutert

Ralph Fiennes, Nora Fingscheidt

Ralph Fiennes will play legendary racehorse trainer Henry Cecil in Nora Fingscheidt’s Unbeaten for Studiocanal, House Productions and Escapade Pictures.

The film is in advanced development, ahead of a projected shoot in 2027.

Unbeaten is based on the true story of Cecil and his champion racehorse Frankel. It will follow Cecil’s final years as he emerges from disgrace, reunites with the love of his life Jane, and begins his partnership with Frankel.

Tony Rushmer, author of The Triumph Of Henry Cecil: The Authorised Biography , is a consultant on the film, with a screenplay by Bash Doran.

It will be produced by Tessa Ross for House and Rory Aitken for Escapade, with 42 also producing. The film has been developed with the support of BBC Film and Access Entertainment.

Studiocanal has fully financed Unbeaten and will release it theatrically in its territories of UK, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Benelux, Australia and New Zealand. Studiocanal is also handling worldwide sales.

Executive producers are Anna Marsh, Ron Halpern and Joe Naftalin for Studiocanal, with Fiennes and Doran.

Fiennes and Ross previously collaborated on Edward Berger’s Conclave , which received eight Oscar nominations including best actor for Fiennes, and won best adapted screenplay for Peter Straughan.

The project also reunites Fingscheidt with Studiocanal, after the director’s 2024 feature The Outrun .

title_original: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York review – John Turturro steals this simple, charming tale
editorial_title_zh: 《纽约唯一的活着的扒手》影评——约翰·特托罗在这部简单迷人的故事中大放异彩
editorial_excerpt_zh: 圣丹斯电影节：在这部节奏闲适、直白、结尾带有反转的犯罪惊悚片中，这位演员饰演了一名从错误之人身上行窃的扒手。诺亚·瑟根（Noah Segan）轻巧的犯罪黑色电影《纽约唯一的活着的扒手》是一部痴迷于……之间代沟的电影……

showing）之作。但他的电影为旧派事物给出了令人信服的理由，这是一部节奏明快、让人回想起70年代风格、由角色驱动的惊悚片，带有借鉴自昔日的复古气魄。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "片名本身部分借用了西蒙和加芬克尔（Simon and Rolls）中，那还是因为那是他自己编剧和导演的。但对于一个值得拥有更多厚重戏份去撕开演的人来说，这是一次受欢迎的晋升，或者说是一次重返巅峰。恰如其分的是，在另一个时代，他本该拥有更加突出的男主角生涯。", "links": [{"text": "John Turturro", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/john-turturro"}], "这基本是一部人们意料之中的电影，但它足够引人入胜，88分钟的片长也十分紧凑。很多时候，那些曾经被视为理所当然的事——用哈利充满深情的回忆来说，就是美好的旧时光——现在感觉就像是个奇迹；正如片名所期待的那样，这是一部非常具有实地取景、能让人认出并指认地标的纽约电影，也是我近期看过的同类电影中最好的一部之一。哈利的生命或许正处于危险之中，但他在城中游荡时有一种迷人的闲逛电影（hangout movie）般的轻快感，不得不抛弃谷歌地图自己找路。尽管与疏远的女儿重聚可能显得略微有些公式化，但它成就了塔提阿娜·玛斯拉尼（Tatiana article_text:
N oah Segan’s light-footed crime noir The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is a film obsessed with the gap between the old and new. There are memories shared about how things used to be, and some older characters refusing to keep up with digital progression, while there are eye-rolls from the younger generation, poking fun at those losing touch with how the world now operates. I’d argue that the theme is often a little overplayed, a classic case of writer-director Segan – a frequent Rian Johnson collaborator – telling rather than showing. But his film makes a convincing case for the old, a brisk throwback to a 70s-era character-led thriller, made with borrowed flair from yesteryear.

The title is itself partly borrowed from a Simon and Garfunkel song and speaks to a protagonist of a dying breed, a pickpocket who prides himself on the old ways; though he might swipe smartphones, he doesn’t own one. He’s played by John Turturro , an actor who hasn’t enjoyed many a lead role of late – his last was in the ill-received Big Lebowski “sequel” The Jesus Rolls and that’s only because he wrote and directed it himself. But this is a welcome step up, or step back up, for someone deserving of something more substantial to tear into. Fittingly, he’s someone who would have arguably had a more prominent career as a leading man in a different time.

His character, Harry, might be straight from a dog-eared crime novel you could fit in your coat pocket – works alone, sticks to his routine, makes for a better thief than he ever did a father – but part of the film’s pleasure lies in the familiar. Nostalgia can become a crutch for so many film-makers but there’s also real sincerity here.

Harry sticks to mostly simple steals, operating on the subway, living in the Bronx but finding most of his work in Manhattan. He sells to an old friend, pawnbroker Ben (fellow Coens collaborator Steve Buscemi), and spends his downtime caring for his wife, who has a degenerative disease that renders her mute and motionless. As is often the case with a character of this ilk, Harry makes the mistake of stealing from the wrong person, the bratty offspring of a connected crime family (rising star Will Price, believably obnoxious), and has to find his way out of a dangerous spot before the day is through.

It’s pretty much the film one expects but it’s engaging enough and tight at 88 minutes. So often, what was once taken for granted – in what Harry would affectionately remember as the good old days – can now feel like a miracle and, as one would hope given the title, this is very much an on-location, recognise-and-point New York film, and one of the best I’ve seen in a while. Harry’s life might be in danger but there’s a charming hangout movie breeziness to his travels around the city, having to find his way without Google Maps. Even though a reunion with his estranged daughter might seem a little too schematic, it allows for a wonderfully effective performance from Tatiana Maslany, who brings decades of anger and sadness into a single scene. She also tells Harry he looks like shit, maybe the film’s most far-fetched moment, given how great Turturro is looking at 68 – a cool but not overstyled man about town – and he’s such a likable, if morally dubious, companion that I would have gladly spent longer with him, stealing from New Yorkers and complaining about prices to anyone who’ll listen.

Segan’s script is not quite as whip-smart as he sometimes seems to think it is and there’s some doubling back “oh you think this happened” explanations that are less fiendishly clever and more goofily contrived. There’s also a surprise last-act cameo from an Oscar-winner that’s a bit too jolting to work given their particularly outsized persona, although Segan does manage a satisfyingly bittersweet ending. It’s an earnest tribute to a lot of things – a city, a time, a genre, a mentality, an actor in Turturro – and while we’ve definitely been here before, it’s nice to come back.

The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is screening at the Sundance film festival and is seeking distribution

article_text:
Voters head to the polls to elect 120 members of the Knesset in an election that will determine whether Benjamin Netanyahu’s rightwing coalition can remain in power. The election is the first to be held since the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023

The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his wife, Sara Netanyahu,cast their ballots at a polling station in JerusalemPhotograph: Yonatan Sindel/AFP/AP

Ultra-Orthodox Jews stand on a street strewn with anti-election pamphlets in the Mea Shearim neighbourhood of JerusalemPhotograph: Kevin Coombs/Reuters

Keith Siegel and Aviva Siegel vote in in Gazit. Three years ago, they were kidnapped from their home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza during the October 7 attacks. Aviva was freed after 51 days in captivity. She then campaigned for the release of her husband, who was freed after 484 daysPhotograph: Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty Images

Mansour Abbas, a Palestinian candidate, Knesset member and leader of the Ra’am party, heads to a polling station with his wife and daughter in MagharPhotograph: Rami Shlush/Reuters

Security personnel with a sniffer dog inspect a school being used as a polling station in the Israeli settlement of Kiryat Arba, in the occupied West Bank, where the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, is expected to votePhotograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

Hotel porters push a luggage trolley past Democrats party supporters near a polling station in central Jerusalem. Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad have returned to vote in this electionPhotograph: Kevin Coombs/Reuters

A supporter of the Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, arranges electoral banners outside a polling station in JerusalemPhotograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images

Ruby Chen and Hagit Chen, parents of Itay Chen, speak at event in Hostage Square, Tel Aviv, commemorating the October 7 2023 Hamas-led attacks. The pair have been urging Israelis to vote for changePhotograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty Images

title_original: Roy Lichtenstein Has Lost His Luster
editorial_title_zh: 罗伊·利希滕斯坦失去了往日光彩
editorial_excerpt_zh: 他从美国理想的讽刺者变成了对自身的恶搞，成了一位满足于借用其他艺术家杰作的艺术家。

article_text:
Art Review

Roy Lichtenstein Has Lost His Luster

He went from being a satirist of America’s ideals to a parody of himself, an artist content with other artists’ masterpieces.

Hyperallergic )

Roy Lichtenstein’s paintings stick in your mind. They are memorable and congenial. When I went to Roy Lichtenstein: Like New , the first major survey of his work in more than 30 years, at the Whitney Museum, I expected to be surprised by something new the curators dug up in their research into the sources of many of the more than 130 paintings, sculptures, drawings, and prints on view. I was not initially disappointed.

Throughout his life, Lichtenstein credited Hoyt Sherman, his teacher at Ohio State University, with teaching him how to see. Lichtenstein gave his first son the middle name “Hoyt” and, after becoming successful, endowed the Hoyt L. Sherman Studio Art Center at the university in the 1990s. Sherman developed an experimental program where students were shown objects briefly in a darkened room and asked to draw them, an experience that is the opposite of traditional life drawing classes. Near the beginning of the exhibition, there is a darkened room with a 15-minute video reenacting one of Sherman’s “Flash Labs.” Artist Alex Da Corte, also one of the curators of the show, acts as Sherman; he wears prosthetics, and playfully teaches the class. Hung on the wall, at different heights, are some of Lichtenstein’s works from the ‘60s.

Da Corte and his team also recreated four murals, including “Greene Street Mural” (1983), which is nearly 100 feet (~30.5 m) in length, and “Super Sunset Billboard” (1967) in the museum’s west-facing window, so museum visitors can time their visit and see two sunsets at once. I think these and other jokes muddied the waters of a famous artist widely celebrated for his charming, emotionally empty (or should I say repressed?) paintings drawn from comic strips, advertising, and paintings by other famous artists, including Pablo Picasso, Claude Monet, and Chinese classical masters such as Mi Youren. Perhaps they didn’t want us to think too long about what happens when charm loses its allure.

article_text:
Nitesh Tiwari’s “ Ramayana : Part One,” starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash , will be available to buy on demand from streamer JioHotstar in India after its theatrical run.

The deal between JioHotstar and Prime Focus Studios will see the film sold as a separate on-demand purchase on the platform. The companies described it as the first pay-per-view offering of its kind on JioHotstar. The film will stream in the best quality each supported device can handle.

Related Stories

'Nick Cannon @ Night' Podcast Moves to BET, Will Relaunch as a Weekly TV Talk Show (EXCLUSIVE)

The epic, starring Ranbir Kapoor, Yash and Sai Pallavi, follows exiled prince Rama (Kapoor) and his consort Sita (Pallavi) through exile into catastrophe, as Sita’s abduction at the hands of Ravana (Yash) sets in motion an epic war between righteousness and evil. Sunny Deol plays Hanuman and Ravie Dubey Lakshman. Arun Govil, Lara Dutta, Rakul Preet Singh, Vivek Oberoi, Kunal Kapoor and Kajal Aggarwal round out the cast.

The film opens worldwide on Nov. 5, in time for the Diwali festival holiday, in the Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and English languages. Imax 3D is among its formats. Sony Pictures Entertainment is releasing the film globally . The film’s Indian distribution will be handled by media personality Karan Johar’s Dharma Productions.

“’Ramayana’ is one of India’s greatest civilizational treasures – a story that has shaped our conscience, inspired our imagination, and guided the way we live for centuries,” said Nita M. Ambani, chair of JioStar. “As India enters a new era of storytelling, we have an extraordinary opportunity to carry our cultural legacy forward. At JioHotstar, our vision is to use technology to bring the finest stories within reach of every Indian. It is our privilege to present this grand cinematic vision of ‘Ramayana’ to families across the country, and introduce a new generation to its eternal values of duty, love, courage, and goodness.”

Prime Focus Studios is producing with DNEG, the visual effects and production company that has won eight Oscars, and Yash’s Monster Mind Creations. “Ramayana” is a live-action project in two parts, with Shridhar Raghavan adapting Valmiki’s epic for the screen.

Namit Malhotra, the producer and filmmaker who founded DNEG and serves as its CEO, said he believes the film should be watched on the largest screen available, in Imax 3D.

“But our country’s cinema infrastructure cannot reach everyone who holds this epic close,” Malhotra said. “’Ramayana’ belongs to every Indian, and our ambition must reflect that. JioHotstar has time and again shown how technology can bring a nation together through its sports and entertainment offering. That made them a natural partner to take Ramayana into people’s hands and living rooms, after its theatrical run.”

The film brings in Oscar winners Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman as composers. Ravi Bansal and Ramsey Avery handled production design, and Terry Notary and Guy Norris oversaw the action. The film was designed with Imax and other premium large formats in mind, and the production mixes Indian and international talent.

article_text:
Films and events

Thrill

Heysel 85

This is a gripping and sobering dramatic reconstruction of the tragedy that unfolded during the 1985 European Cup final between Liverpool and Juventus at the Brussels stadium.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Teodora Ana Mihai

Screenwriters Lode Desmet, Isabelle Darras, Teodora Ana Mihai

With Violet Braeckman, Matteo Simoni, Josse De Pauw

Belgium-Netherlands-Germany 2026. 92min

Courtesy of Icon Film Distribution

Languages Dutch, French, English, Italian With English subtitles

Certificate BBFC12A

Introduction

Teodora Ana Mihai rightly leaves the match off screen to focus on the ordeal endured by hundreds of fans. The film also channels its outrage at events that live television had no access to: the sloppy pre-match planning, the slow response and pathetic handling of the catastrophe and the irresponsible power play that shaped those dreadful, fateful hours.

Sergio Fant

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

The Match

Few sporting contests loom as large in the public imagination as the dramatic 1986 World Cup Quarter Final between England and Argentina, as this documentary details.

The Meltdown

Sutherland Award winner Manuela Martelli delivers a knife-edge thriller centring on the disappearance of a teenager in a remote Chilean resort.

Black Church Bay

In a sleepy Welsh fishing village, Barry’s life starts to unravel after an intimate encounter in this gripping mystery drama starring Tom Cullen and Joe Locke.

article_text:
In 2021, 10 months after Myanmar’s military overthrew the democratically elected government in a coup, Canadian photojournalist Bryan Dickie heard of a rare opening to access the country. He acted swiftly. The experience of that trip inspired him to enlist long-time collaborators Robert Mentov and Dwight Jantzi, with the trio returning to Myanmar two years later and capturing the training regime of young recruits of the People’s Defense Force. The result of the six weeks on the ground is “ White Tiger Column ,” opening this year’s International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam.

Related Stories

Keanu Reeves to Star in Netflix Action Movie 'Maelstrom' After Alan Ritchson Drops Out

Keira Knightley and 'Black Doves' Creator Joe Barton on Why Helen Should Have Been the One to Kill [SPOILER], That Oner and Hopes for Season 3

For 45 days, the trio of filmmakers captured the lives of trainees and commanders as they readied to leave for the front and join the war. Through an observational lens, the directors reflect on the dichotomy of the situation: the mundanity of the lives of young kids who scroll on TikTok and sing mindlessly to Taylor Swift and Justin Bieber and the harsh reality of armed combat.

Speaking with Variety ahead of heading to Amsterdam, Dickie mentions how he built “deep ties” with locals in Myanmar over 15 years of covering the area as a photojournalist. That, coupled with his close relationship with the Burmese diaspora in Canada, gave the filmmaker great knowledge of the country’s geopolitical situation. “I’ve also embedded with multiple different ethnic armed organizations over the years, so through all of that I built up a bit of a track record going into these areas.”

“We just felt a clear creative collaboration,” adds Jantzi of the early days of working on the project. “Upon landing on the ground and shooting alongside each other, we were just working very closely, day by day, developing our shot list and working through our potential narrative arcs. Through Rob and my ongoing work as filmmakers and then Bryan and his deep knowledge of the context and the region, it just felt like a very cohesive, natural fit to work together.”

Jantzi emphasizes the trio would have loved to have taken a few more trips to the country during development and shooting, but the situation was too precarious to allow the extra time. “The reality is that the situation changes so much week by week that you can’t even really plan your characters six months ahead,” he notes. “We got extremely lucky with timing and kept trying to extend our trip, and things kept changing and becoming a bit more contentious in the region.”

That sensitivity extends to the subject of the documentary itself, with the directors keenly aware of the cultural and political nuances the project involved. Mentov mentions how the trio worked closely with the diaspora, as well as fellow Burmese filmmakers on the ground. “One thing we wanted to do was to maintain this observational approach.”

“Essentially, we were just dropped into this jungle,” he goes on. “We were trying to understand it, but it was very similar to how the recruits were: dropped into the jungle and trying to understand it all. Cinematically, we really just wanted to film these conversations at a distance and give space for them as opposed to trying to drive a narrative in more of a traditional documentary style.”

That desire is clearly reflected in the film’s visual and narrative language, with “White Tiger Column” foregoing traditional talking heads or extensive voice-overs cueing the viewer into minute details of the conflict in favor of letting the camera linger on seemingly mundane activities made poignant in this very specific context. The filmmakers also shot on longer lenses and employed a locked-off tripod technique to keep the camera static for stretched periods.

Another “conscious” decision was to avoid showcasing explicit violence, with the film focusing instead on the training and conversations revolving around conflict. “We talked a lot about wanting to make a war film that didn’t show war,” notes Dickie.

“I found it very hard to get people outside of the region to wrap their head around what is going on there because it’s so complicated and the bar of entry for understanding is quite high,” he adds. “With this documentary, we tried to switch our approach where instead of trying to explain or go into the hard details of Myanmar’s history and culture, what we did was focus on the universal, human themes like sovereignty, freedom and missing home.”

This also spoke to our current political moment, where younger generations are taking central roles in political movements across the world. “White Tiger Column” opens IDFA mere weeks after Brazil re-elected Lula following historic demonstrations kickstarted by students from the Fluminense Federal University, and Serbia’s long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić was overthrown by a student-led protest movement in the country’s snap parliamentary elections. Young people were also decisive in the recent midterm elections in the U.S., with the second-highest youth turnout in a midterm election in 30 years.

“Revolution is on the lips of a lot of people,” says Dickie, with Jantzi adding: “We just hope this can be a portrait of what revolution could look like around the world. If democracy were to fall, would we have the courage and the power to fight? Over the years, there’s been this conversation about Gen Z and Gen Alpha not having what older generations had, but I think this picture of these kids leaving it all behind—video games, comfort—to fight for the future of their country is so beautiful.”

Dickie intervenes to say that “the Spring Revolution in Myanmar is a very pure grassroots revolution and quite anarchic,” but it is also a “bit of a Catch-22.” “Although it is a beautiful revolution, at the end of the day, it is a revolution. I talk to these guys weekly; they are still in the jungle fighting. People are still dying in the mud. They are still being bombed from the sky. When talking about revolution, you can get caught up in the theory of it and the flowery language, but at the end of the day, this is war.”

“White Tiger Column” is produced by Tom Edgerton for Lightwood Green in co-production with Nocte Films and Rugio!

article_text:
“I have this problem ,” shares Errol Morris , the Oscar-winning documentary filmmaker behind “The Thin Blue Line,” “The Fog of War” and countless other renowned docs. You see, the 78-year-old can’t seem to screen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s docu-phenomenon on Elizabeth Holmes , “You Can See Everything.” He claims to have contacted the appropriate parties but has thus far been rebuffed. “Can you get me a screener?” he pleads. (I cannot.)

Related Stories

Harry Styles 'Together, Together' Tour Doc Coming From John Wilson, Universal Pictures Content Group (EXCLUSIVE)

Harry Styles Waltzes His Way Through 'Coming Up Roses' Music Video

What Morris did do, however, was finally watch Alex Gibney’s 2019 documentary on Holmes and her sham blood-testing company Theranos — “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley” — for the very first time.

Morris, who’s directed “probably 1,000” commercials for various companies, was hired by Holmes in 2015 to shoot a series of ads for Theranos that depicted the “founder” staring wide-eyed into the camera that have attracted criticism for contributing to her mythmaking . Morris says he doesn’t know how Gibney got ahold of extra footage from the ads to use in “The Inventor,” but that’s not all: Morris exclusively revealed to Variety that he actually conducted a two-hour Interrotron interview with Holmes that he’s contemplating releasing in light of the renewed interest around the infamous grifter.

I never really wanted to see it until recently for a variety of different reasons, and I was quite surprised to find out that I was in it.

Well, what’s really not known about any of this is, yes, I did all the advertising for Theranos, but I did it at a time when Elizabeth Holmes was on the front cover of Forbes and many other magazines. She was riding high, and this was before everything collapsed. Did I have any reason to believe that she was a fraud? I did not. Did that change as time went on? It did. I had tried very hard, over a number of years, to do a documentary on Elizabeth Holmes and it would have happened except that she was under indictment. There was massive litigation going on.

I asked her, at a certain point, if I could film an interview with her — and this is at the height of her success — and I did film a two-hour interview with her, which is not very well-known if it is known at all. And I just watched that. I am sincerely interested in putting that out as an unedited film.

If anything, it gives you a comparison of Elizabeth before and Elizabeth after , which I think is interesting in and of itself. I noticed that the Gibney film begins and ends with my interview with Elizabeth Holmes.

Well, myself and the people in my office, but yes, for all intents and purposes, it has not been seen by anyone. Let me ask you a fast question: Why do you think [“ You Can See Everything ”] has proven so popular?

Well, it’s hard for me to tell you about the film having not yet seen it, but I can tell you what I think about Elizabeth Holmes having spent a considerable amount of time with her. I was interviewed by John Carreyrou recently for an article that subsequently appeared in The New York Times, and he was questioning me about something I’d said to him many, many years ago when I was considering making a documentary about Elizabeth Holmes and had asked him if he would participate in that documentary. Some people see these stories as an on/off switch of she’s innocent or she’s guilty, she’s lying or she’s telling the truth. And when you’re investigating a crime, part of that investigation has to be if the person is guilty or innocent, since the criminal justice system works in such a way that you are looking for some kind of result. But what interests me is: To what extent was she self-deceived? To what extent did she believe in her own bullshit? Carreyrou understandably wants to tell you that she knowingly committed fraud, is guilty, should have been convicted and is in prison, as she should be. I keep wondering about the psychology of self-deception because part of me believes that she believes in Theranos and that she could achieve the results as promised.

Yes, it is. You could say that lots of people in Silicon Valley misrepresent or out-and-out lie about what their technology can achieve, but in this case it involved medical results and people whose lives are directly affected by those medical results, and that in itself makes it different.

Now, we can get into a philosophical discussion of the nature of lying and what is a lie, and did she lie in a very clear sense? Yes. Many, many times. Did she see them as lies? That is of interest to me.

Probably the Robert Bresson “Joan of Arc,” which is one of my very favorite films.

The nature of her punishment is not similar to being burned at the stake, and if you thought that’s what I meant by it, I did not.

One thing I can say about Joan of Arc: Do I think that God was speaking to her? I have a confession to make: I don’t believe in God. Do I think that God exists? No, I don’t! Do I think that God was directly communicating with Joan of Arc? I don’t! Do I think she thought that God was directly communicating with her? She did! She went to the stake on the basis of it. That’s your comparison.

—Don’t call them promos! I was hired as a commercial director, and I’ve shot probably 1,000 commercials. In the Gibney documentary, it is mentioned that Elizabeth Holmes and Patrick O’Neill, who was her CCO, had hired me because of the many Apple commercials I’d directed for Steve Jobs. If I had known how much of my interview was being used [by Gibney], or even if it was being used at all, I’m not sure what I would have said. I knew it was being used, but I never really wanted to watch [“The Inventor”]. Maybe I’d just had enough of it.

This I do not know. I really don’t know. And I’m not being coy or cagey. I do not know.

People have never seen my long interview that I did with Elizabeth Holmes. I’ve heard that I have been accused of representing a fraud — knowingly — and this is just not true. I’ll join a lot of other people who were on the Theranos board at the time that I was doing this series of commercials.

I actually interviewed Henry Kissinger just before he died.

It might. I have so much stuff that I do nothing with.

I believe that’s true!

You tell me and I’ll tell you if it’s real!

That’s it! And of course, they said no. Fortunately, enough people have said yes over the years, but I can’t tell you how many people have said no. I once said to my producer for commercials, “You know, I get all these commercials, but I’ve never gotten diarrhea or erectile dysfunction commercials. What’s wrong with me?” I once got a Depend commercial, and my ideas for incontinence/Depend commercials were by and large rejected.

Thank you for asking. I had just done a long interview with Janis Karpinski, who’d just been demoted in connection with Abu Ghraib — and this interview has never seen the light of day — so there’s this lady general inside a tank in a war zone. Shells are exploding all around. The tank is on maneuvers. We see the face of the lady general inside the tank. She has an enormously pinched expression. She is fidgety, edgy. And then, you hear the sound of running water, and the expression on her face changes to one of total relaxation and pleasure. And then we cut outside and we see the artillery exploding. Depend .

The guy who was producing the commercials to Depend put his face two inches away from mine and said, “THERE IS NOTHING, NOTHING FUNNY ABOUT INCONTINENCE!” And I said, “I guess I beg to differ.”

Because the company fell apart and she was prosecuted… but I can’t really answer it. The clearest answer is that I’d moved on. But now I feel pretty strongly that this is an interesting document — not because I’m trying to prove something about Elizabeth Holmes, but it does provide some kind of evidence of what she was like when everything was going her way.

That she was a true believer.

article_text:
The women of “ The Gilded Age ” are assembled in the lavishly appointed drawing room of the Fifth Avenue Hotel for a postmortem.

“I’m still buzzing from the other night,” Marceline Hugot, who plays Mrs. Foster, the director of the Heritage Society, says as she rises to address the group. “Despite some hiccups, President Cleveland was charmed.”

With that, the camera pulls back, and Gladys Russell (Taissa Farmiga) enters, eliciting upturned eyebrows and side glances as she makes excuses for her absent mother, Bertha Russell, whose rise to the top of society has consumed much of the HBO series’ three previous seasons. But as she begins to describe the headache that has waylaid Bertha, Farmiga’s words grow entangled, and she blows her lines.

“Damn it,” Farmiga exclaims, using a word that would cause any one of these ladies who lunch to stagger back toward their settee in shock.

Cut.

Farmiga grabs her script. Races through the dialogue out loud. Then exits the room to make her entrance again as a makeup artist appears to administer touch-ups and a wardrobe assistant swoops in to adjust one of the women’s hats. As fans of the show know, every detail on “ The Gilded Age ” has to be just right. Bringing the 19th century to life requires a small army of costumers, builders, technicians, and researchers. And Season 4, which debuts on Nov. 1, is the biggest yet. There are multiple weddings, a party at a dance hall, a parade, an inventors’ convention, the dedication of a national monument, and, yes, a presidential visit.

“Usually we have two or three events like this in a season,” said Bob Shaw, the show’s production designer. “This is the season where we keep saying, ‘it’s go big or go home.'”

The larger canvas is the reward for a ratings surge that saw “The Gilded Age,” which had languished on the bubble for its first two years, finally become appointment television. Cast members first noticed the rising interest on social media, then grew accustomed to strangers approaching them on the street to share their thoughts on Gladys’s relationship woes or George Russell’s latest corporate battle.

“It’s so rare that you let a show be on the air for a few years to find its audience,” Carrie Coon , who plays Bertha, told IndieWire. “Our attention moves on more quickly now, and I have friends on amazing shows that no one’s watching, so to know that people are actually consuming the thing you’re making is very gratifying. There’s been this uptick in people recognizing us and saying how much they love the show. It’s all over the world. It’s all socioeconomic classes. It’s every end of the political spectrum. There are fans in every corner.”

Co-creator Sonja Warfield realized “The Gilded Age” had broken through after her parents attended a funeral.

“All these people were hovering around my dad and mom,” she said. “And they didn’t want to talk about the deceased; they wanted to discuss ‘The Gilded Age.'”

There was certainly plenty for fans to unpack. After working in tandem to bring New York to heel, the Russells’ marriage came undone, with George (Morgan Spector) furious that Bertha had manipulated her daughter into marrying a duke. There was also an assassination attempt, multiple engagements, a Newport ball, and several changes in fortune (families are always rising and falling in Julian Fellowes ‘ America). Online, the conversation intensified, and thirsty memes sprouted (George was dubbed “Railroad Daddy,” and Ben Ahlers’ servant-turned-inventor was christened “Clock Twink “). Warfield has a theory for why it took fans a few years to catch up with the period drama.

“Season 3 is the sweet spot for TV series,” Warfield said. “Season 1, you’re establishing the world. Season 2, you’re starting to build out the plot lines. And Season 3, the actors really know the characters and the writers know the nuances of the actors. We can write to their strengths. And that gives us more real estate for their characters’ journeys.”

For the first time, Warfield and Fellowes are entering a new season with confidence it won’t be their last. They haven’t mapped out where the Russells, the Scotts and the van Rhijns go from here, but they believe there are more stories left to tell as America enters a new age.

“We have a Season 5 in us if we’re allowed to do it,” Fellowes said. “But when you write a TV series, you have to finish every season so that it could be the end, because one day it will be.”

There’s plenty of backstabbing, social snobbery, and romantic complications to go around this season. Coon and Spector choose their words carefully, hesitant to reveal anything that flirts with being a spoiler, but they promise that the Russells’ marital problems won’t be resolved any time soon. Without his wife by his side, George, so confident in his business dealings and so adept at outmaneuvering the old-money elites whose hold on American enterprise is loosening, is unmoored. As his empire begins to teeter, he turns to dangerous ways of coping.

“George is a disaster without Bertha,” Spector said. “He’s doing everything he can to fill the void.”

Bertha is equally disoriented without her supportive spouse, but Coon believes that her character was justified in pressuring Gladys to marry royalty. The match may have been arranged, with Gladys offering wealth and the duke respectability, but as the season dawns, the couple is deeply in love. Bertha’s daughter’s future isn’t just secure — it’s bright.

“I’ve always maintained that Bertha was absolutely right,” Coon said. “She’s a good judge of character, and she really liked the Duke.”

Season 4 also promises big things for Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), the Black journalist who spent much of the first two seasons dealing with personal tragedy or bearing witness to racial violence, as she did during a trip to the South that ended with a lynch mob. But last season, Peggy fell head over heels for Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica), and the new episodes find the well-off Scott family navigating an even higher rung of Black society as they prepare for the kind of blowout wedding that the white characters are constantly attending.

“It’s wonderful to see Black joy on television,” said Audra McDonald, who plays Peggy’s mother. “We had a lot of drama and tragedy in the first couple of seasons for the Scotts, and it’s wonderful to see them emerge in this way. It’s exciting to see Peggy come out of this cocoon to become an iron butterfly.”

Then there’s Ada (Cynthia Nixon) and Agnes ( Christine Baranski ), who may live across the street from the Russells, but whose family line traces back to the Mayflower, making them ambassadors of the old order their new-money neighbors are threatening. Agnes once controlled the purse strings, but her wayward son Oscar (Blake Ritson) fell for a Ponzi scheme, costing them their fortune. In an only-on “The Gilded Age” coincidence, Ada came into a sizable inheritance at the exact same moment, allowing the family to retain their mansion. The role reversal comes to a head this season when Ada is expected to foot the bill for Agnes’ grand soirée for the president.

“She’s getting more comfortable with her stature, with being a woman of means, and with being the head of the household,” Nixon said.

And Baranski hints that Agnes, whose haughty putdowns are beloved by “Gilded Age” fans, gets to go in unexpected directions.

“It’s my favorite year in terms of my character’s narrative line,” she said. “I’ve never enjoyed myself more, and I’m just so grateful to the writers. Agnes’ sense of identity is challenged this season. I get to do some really powerful scenes.”

“The Gilded Age” has taken hold of the culture just as a new billionaire set is flexing their muscles. The characters on their show made their fortunes in railroads and oil, this new gang of robber barons controls everything from AI to electric cars and social networks. The parallels are hard to ignore, and some cast members seem uncomfortable lionizing rapacious capitalists while we are living through a new gilded age that seems nastier and more brutish.

“It’s so bizarre,” Nixon said. “These billionaires are the main story of our moment, and it is the main story of ‘The Gilded Age.” You have these people who appear seemingly out of nowhere and have so much money, and because of their incredible wealth and their quest for more, they are destroying everything from the planet to democracy to the Constitution, you name it.”

Fellowes acknowledges that the show romanticizes a kind of swashbuckling industrialist, but he thinks that their legacy is complicated.

“I do feel I’m sticking up for them,” Fellowes said. “If you watch a series and someone comes in who’s a millionaire from Wall Street, you know he’s the baddie. I’m a lone voice in the other direction, because I think the Gilded Age was a very exciting time for America, and these men made it exciting. They built an economy that put America at the peace table with the loudest voice in both of the coming world wars, when it had only existed as a country for one and a half centuries. I’m perfectly happy to protect people who can’t protect themselves. So I don’t want to seem as if I only support the robber barons. I don’t. But the fashion now is to hate them, and we ought to remember that they got America ready for the 20th century.”

Back on set, the cast and crew of “The Gilded Age” are entering their third hour of capturing the post-presidential visit discussion from every angle, and they’re getting punchy. Beneath their corsets, stomachs are starting to growl, and they’re eager to break for lunch. In between setups, Baranski tries to keep her energy up, scrunching her face and blowing her lips together to keep them elastic.

“This is better than a sharp stick in the eye,” Baranski tells the table as the camera crew gets ready for another shot. “I always wanted to say that while accepting an award.”

Despite the long hours (most of the actors had to arrive just after 5 a.m. to begin the hourslong process of getting in costume), “The Gilded Age” cast can’t believe that after being counted out for several seasons, they have finally, at long last, climbed to the top.

“We hope we get a fifth, a sixth, or a seventh season,” Donna Murphy, who plays Caroline Astor, said. “There’s been this gradual kind of gelling and coalescing as a company. We just keep getting better. I remember at the end of filming the third season, Christine turned to me and said, ‘I could do this for the rest of my life.’ And you know what, she’s right.”
excerpt_original: Carrie Coon, Cynthia Nixon, Morgan Spector, Julian Fellowes and more on the marital problems, blowout parties, and social scandals in store for the HBO hit.

article_text:
Films and events

Dare

Chronicles from the Siege

Winner of the Best First Feature Award at the Berlin International Film Festival this year, Abdallah Al-Khatib’s fiction debut traces the daily lives of Palestinian citizens trapped in a war zone.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Abdallah Al-Khatib

With Nadim Rimawi, Saja Kilani, Ahmed Zitouni

Algeria-France-Palestine 2026. 98min

Courtesy of Loco Films

Language Arabic With English subtitles

Introduction

In this bold and defiant film, divided into five interconnected stories, the occupants of a military-occupied war zone find the foundational things in life – food, sex, safely giving birth – become matters of life and death as they scrabble for survival. Al-Kahtib’s film is an articulate reminder of the importance of connection, even in the darkest of times.

Grace Barber-Plentie

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Mariinka

Shot over ten years, this unflinching portrait of youth in Eastern Ukraine is a rare and powerful account of the passing of time during conflict.

Concrete Land

Asmahan Bkerat’s feature directorial debut is an intimate, multi-generational portrait of a mixed-raced family fighting displacement and hostility in Jordan.

Az Zeeb

Discovering a cache of Super 8 home movies and photographs following the death of his grandmother, Chilean filmmaker Rafael Guendelman embarks on a personal journey through his family’s intertwined political histories.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Between crafting ceramics, farming and housebuilding, one man has built a life in art; and he wants others to do the same"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On a slight hill overlooking a set of small fields growing rice and lotus, not far from the sea in rural Chiba, Japan, a cluster of clay pots sits in the grass. Slumped on their sides, they’re bulbous, distended vessels half a metre in diameter, their surfaces in muted reds, browns and yellows, pocked with fingerprints and the occasional swirl of circular brushwork patterning. Japanese artist Kazunori Hamana makes these ceramics, but he emphasises that they sit equally alongside his activities of farming and fixing up abandoned houses in the area; their position outside in the summer sun, flecked with dirt and home to spiders and grasshoppers, seems indicative of his attitude towards them – not quite dismissive, but part of the landscape. A figure who has been planting rice and messing with pots for the past few decades, as if in anticipation of contemporary art’s popular turn to clay and the rural, Hamana came to the designation of artist seemingly reluctantly, only after a series of past lives: graduating from an agriculture high school in 1988 before attending university in San Diego, running a sneaker shop and a restaurant in Tokyo’s Harajuku neighbourhood during the 1990s, then moving to Chiba towards the end of the 2000s, fishing anchovy and later growing rice, while taking up as a self-taught ceramicist."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "From his perch on the edge of the Atlantic, the ceramics proved popular enough to establish Hamana as an artist exhibiting internationally during the mid 2010s as part of a wave of ceramics held up as ‘new mingei’ – a contemporary approach to folk craft and ceramics – showing with international galleries such as Blum & Poe (before its closure). What this enabled, in turn, was Hamana’s larger practice, which has the aim of creating a rural space in which artists can live and work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The artist residency Commons/Oppes (‘oppes’ meaning ‘push’ in the local dialect) is an attempt at community creation and a practical response to Japan’s depopulated countrysides, taking advantage of empty buildings that dot the prefecture. It’s also a determinedly independent endeavour, setting it apart from the state-funded regional festivals and biennials that define much of Japan’s contemporary art outside the urban centres. Hosting artists for one to three months at a time, in a set of houses that Hamana and a group of friends and helpers have fixed up, residents get on with their own practices, but also often end up taking part in the rhythms of rural life: helping to plant rice or weed the paddies, chopping down bamboo or picking plums when these come into season. While the residency only officially began this year, it’s been in motion for almost a decade, with friends and residents attending informally in recent years. What struck me when visiting in May this year and again in August was that already several artists and previous residents had relocated to the area, an artist village in the making. A handful of other houses for residents are near completion, while one smaller hut recently finished holds a kitchen designed to host artists and creatives focusing on food. A correlated strand of the residency, Commons/Kuwa, launched in August, with Shizuoka-based artist Takayuki Watanabe devising a series of events over a week, including mochimaking. Sitting in Hamana’s house, among half-finished pots on the floor, overlooking a rice field waiting to be harvested the following week, we spoke about nostalgia, beauty and the end of capitalism."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/DSC6198-copy-1230x1845.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Photo: Noboru Murata. Courtesy Commons/Oppes, Chiba", "credit": "ArtReview"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ArtReview Asia Where did the idea for the residency and countryside community start for you?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Kazunori Hamana My uncle married a farmer’s daughter, and we went to her house when I was three. We still have the photo, it was 1973. We came into a house with a high grass roof and carved wooden beams, I was so shocked. I couldn’t speak, but I thought ‘What is this? What is this beauty, compared to my house?’ At six years old, I told my mother I wanted to build a house like that. And she said, ‘What? You crazy?’ My grandfather was a carpenter and I asked him if we could make a chicken coop. So we built a house together, and he bought a baby chicken too. I was so satisfied, going around outside with the chicken. I was a crazy kid. So I had always the idea of a rural life. Not so much as a farmer as occupation, but a handcrafted life, with nature. It wasn’t taught, my father or mother never told me. It was an intuition."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA When did that idea of rural life start to meet with the conception of a creative community?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH Community came much later. First, it’s an individual question, a presence with nature. I was sick of living in the city. I escaped from my family when I was fifteen years old to a rural area, I stayed with a couple of farmers and went to agriculture school. Then I learned, with the other students, a different kind of sharing and relationship, a new kind of community or family. It wasn’t by design; accidentally, I was with other people in the middle of nature, I could go fishing, skateboarding, cycling and study. It let me come back to myself. Since then I continue to make sure I connect with nature and our ancestors’ handmade culture."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA Sounds idyllic, though these ancestors don’t just seem to be Japanese farmers for you; you worked with vintage clothing for a period, and in other interviews you’ve spoken about your appreciation for denim as an ‘American mingei’ or folkcraft in itself. How are these things related for you?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH In the late 1970s or early 80s I would go shopping with my mother, but I didn’t like anything she chose. Every garment. I hated it all. At that time, it was all nylon and polyester in Japan. Then, when I was eleven years old, I found Converse, canvas shoes made in the USA. It was totally different, better quality. I found Levi’s 501: work clothes, well-crafted, thick material, 100 percent cotton. We didn’t have that kind of clothing here. So I started going to clothes shops by myself, and I started collecting T-shirts and sweatshirts like the Champion reverse-weave. Eighties Japan was terrible. Everything my mother chose was classic of the time, but plastic. The new thing was better. Handcrafting had been forgotten; an aesthetic and an aesthetic intuition had been lost. How can I explain it? We see the ocean, or sunlight, and we think it’s beautiful: this is aesthetic intuition. This kind of aesthetic I found in Levi’s 501s."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA Levi’s also based its brand on a rugged cowboy image, and a sort of idealised vision of American countryside. What role does nostalgia play in this return to a rural lifestyle?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH About every 30 years, we feel nostalgia for a past time. Vintage is a big trend now, but it’s also looking for more story and craftsmanship apart from the mass production of Uniqlo or Zara. It’s not a return to the past, but about looking for a better balance. Of course, I use a smartphone and drive a car. The reality is we are losing physical relationships and the connection to nature. Everything is too industrial; industry is, of course, important, but not too much. It’s the same with capitalism: we need it, but its purpose is just about making more money than other people; about trying to be famous; and just to consume, consume, consume. But that’s not a true purpose, because you’re never satisfied. It’s just like, what’s new? Look at Netflix, TikTok. There are a thousand times more movies today, but they all look the same. We have to hurry, we have to watch more. People get bored anyway in one second, so why spend the time making something better? I don’t think that before the 1950s, or during the nineteenth century, or under feudal society everything was perfect, or everyone back then was a genius, but you had to spend more time and e²ort making something. People were more sensitive because they weren’t as addicted to consumption. For me, it’s all connected, because my purpose is to try to find beauty every day; there is satisfaction in that. Now I collect abandoned houses. But the old farmhouses are similar to 501s. To work hard, you need tough clothes. A house is the same, you know? Handcrafted materials, built physically to be better. You have to cut wood, and do it all analogue. Building up old-style houses each day is an opportunity to try to be better: that’s art for me."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/DSC_3925-1230x812.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "‘Ginnan’, one of three residences at Commons/Oppes, Chiba. Photo: Noboru Murata. Courtesy Commons/Oppes, Chiba", "credit": "ArtReview"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/LINE_ALBUM_2026写真　携帯撮影_260723_391.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Interior of ‘Nobuki’ residence. Courtesy Commons/Oppes, Chiba", "credit": "ArtReview"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA While that work and your farming is situated in the Chiba landscape, your ceramics are exhibited in New York, London, Los Angeles. What is that kind of art for you?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH For me art is creating. So of course I’m doing exhibitions, art fairs, but it’s not the main purpose for me. It’s nice to share time with the audience and sometimes someone buys something. That’s a wonderful thing, but it’s not my priority. I like making things; someone else might think my creation is art and want to share the piece."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA So it’s their choice if they see it as art. How did you come to making ceramics?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH People appreciate my work like a sculpture, but I would say it’s more a result of my activity of fixing houses, making communities, my respect for handcrafted methods. The pots are not art, they are a leftover from those activities. Twenty-eight years ago I started living in front of the ocean, both to be able to ignore the business mindset and for my own happiness. I started catching fish, I spent three months making a fishing net, for my own satisfaction and intuition. Making the pots was the same, I wanted to make a natural thing. It was a lot of fun and joy. I didn’t have a plan; I was not going to sell them. Later I started growing rice, and the rice is not for sale. It’s similar. As a result of making, some people started buying the ceramics, and I invest that money into the houses. But exhibitions, the market, that’s not my purpose; my main purpose is the day-to-day of challenging myself."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA The question of circulation comes to mind; the ceramics circulating enable the community here to circulate, and they kind of orbit each other in a certain way. But usually, for an art career, it’s about awareness of a practice or maker in the first place. There’s lots of self-taught artists who never sell anything, and it’s one thing working here, farming rice and making pots, and then also being featured in The New York Times or Vogue Japan , as you have been. How did the ceramics begin to circulate in that way?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH I did the ceramics for a long time before I showed people. I first shared these online, on Tumblr in the 2010s, shooting the ceramics on my camera at the beach house in front of the ocean. It was very wild and seemed to touch a subconscious demand in people; the wood, the clay, the basic thing of touching mud."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/LINE_ALBUM_2026写真　携帯撮影_260723_95-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Clearing weeds near the rice paddies. Courtesy Commons/Oppes, Chiba", "credit": "ArtReview"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA So it began as an image distributed online?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH It wasn’t an art context, and clay wasn’t at that point as popular in art: handcrafts weren’t really seen as high art. Many followers started on Tumblr, mostly from New York at the time. Conversations with artists started on DMs, like Takayuki Watanabe, who is doing an event in the kitchen here, and Takashi Murakami, who wanted to show a new Japanese craft movement to a us audience. So it ended up in an art context."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA How important is the wild countryside context in the white-walled gallery where these pieces end up sometimes?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH I made it in context, with the ocean and nature. It’s a remaining trace, the context is carried within the object. Some people have said to me that they see what I’m doing, making rice, building community, as an ideal thing for humans to do. And they feel that, but they cannot do it themselves, so they see my work as omamori – a good luck charm."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA How do you feel about being a good luck charm? Is there a sense of performing a kind of ideal countryside for city dwellers?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH Maybe it’s true. Maybe that’s why people appreciate my life and my work, but that’s also a kind of result. I can’t save people, but I can be an alternative example. Things are also changing; over a decade ago, I started talking about community building and fixing. In the artworld here, the emphasis then was on the concept in an artwork, the art-history context, and the artist producing painting, sculptures, artworks where the idea is in the physical piece. Talking about Commons/Oppes, people told me, “You cannot be an artist if you keep doing this. Why go the long way?” They didn’t understand my goal; they thought I was lazy, wasting opportunities. But I didn’t follow this system. I was spending time making rice, trying to build a new type of community. The art market is just a market. My life as an artist is not focusing on the market or sculpture; it’s challenging everything to be better, to find more beautiful things. This challenge is art. After ten years I’ve done a lot of things I planned for a long time, and now they see. And how people are talking about art is changing, especially after the pandemic. Before it was concept and object, now it’s… how can I explain it? I cannot explain. It’s vibes."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/DSC7307-1230x1230.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Kazunori Hamana at work. Photo: Noboru Murata. Courtesy Commons/Oppes, Chiba", "credit": "ArtReview"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA Within that daily process and challenge, where the ceramics are a byproduct, why is it this form of a large vase particularly that you keep returning to?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH I tried many shapes and, of course, I still want to try different shapes. In Japan you often see the tsubo shape, often smaller, practical vases for seeds or food storage. But at a local museum decades ago I saw an old pot with a beautiful organic line to it, and it was a striking size. I found out it was a funeral pot for children, made to fit the body of the child. I felt something close to the mind of the parents. So for now I’m making this; I don’t know about next year. But this shape is a kind of symbol of a parent’s, a human’s love."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA There’s a living-museum aspect to what you’re doing: actively trying out ways of living to see what happens, drawing on the past but mixed in with aspects of the present. In terms of the structures you’re fixing up, it’s not all old farmhouses but a range of eras, older and more recent. Most of the older architecture preserved in Japan is castles and homes of the wealthier parts of society, creating a certain vision of the past. What do you feel you’re building here?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH I’m trying to rewrite the nostalgia, so it’s not just a rich-person aesthetic. We made a mess from the 1970s to today, the buildings were very ugly, all plastic inside. Now, people just demolish, demolish, demolish. But demolishing 1970s buildings is not the answer. It’s easy to demolish and build. But if you keep building new, do you really have an aesthetic? We have to understand why we are lost. What kind of mistakes did we make? And what shouldn’t we do?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARA Also, whose aesthetic? I mean, yes, most humans can agree a sunset is beautiful. But then with architecture, or art, it gets a little bit more difficult."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "KH The most important thing to me is a connection with nature. I’m not just keeping ugly houses, I’m arranging parts of them to make sure we can connect again to what’s outside and around us.
