article_text:
Between crafting ceramics, farming and housebuilding, one man has built a life in art; and he wants others to do the same

On a slight hill overlooking a set of small fields growing rice and lotus, not far from the sea in rural Chiba, Japan, a cluster of clay pots sits in the grass. Slumped on their sides, they’re bulbous, distended vessels half a metre in diameter, their surfaces in muted reds, browns and yellows, pocked with fingerprints and the occasional swirl of circular brushwork patterning. Japanese artist Kazunori Hamana makes these ceramics, but he emphasises that they sit equally alongside his activities of farming and fixing up abandoned houses in the area; their position outside in the summer sun, flecked with dirt and home to spiders and grasshoppers, seems indicative of his attitude towards them – not quite dismissive, but part of the landscape. A figure who has been planting rice and messing with pots for the past few decades, as if in anticipation of contemporary art’s popular turn to clay and the rural, Hamana came to the designation of artist seemingly reluctantly, only after a series of past lives: graduating from an agriculture high school in 1988 before attending university in San Diego, running a sneaker shop and a restaurant in Tokyo’s Harajuku neighbourhood during the 1990s, then moving to Chiba towards the end of the 2000s, fishing anchovy and later growing rice, while taking up as a self-taught ceramicist.

From his perch on the edge of the Atlantic, the ceramics proved popular enough to establish Hamana as an artist exhibiting internationally during the mid 2010s as part of a wave of ceramics held up as ‘new mingei’ – a contemporary approach to folk craft and ceramics – showing with international galleries such as Blum & Poe (before its closure). What this enabled, in turn, was Hamana’s larger practice, which has the aim of creating a rural space in which artists can live and work.

The artist residency Commons/Oppes (‘oppes’ meaning ‘push’ in the local dialect) is an attempt at community creation and a practical response to Japan’s depopulated countrysides, taking advantage of empty buildings that dot the prefecture. It’s also a determinedly independent endeavour, setting it apart from the state-funded regional festivals and biennials that define much of Japan’s contemporary art outside the urban centres. Hosting artists for one to three months at a time, in a set of houses that Hamana and a group of friends and helpers have fixed up, residents get on with their own practices, but also often end up taking part in the rhythms of rural life: helping to plant rice or weed the paddies, chopping down bamboo or picking plums when these come into season. While the residency only officially began this year, it’s been in motion for almost a decade, with friends and residents attending informally in recent years. What struck me when visiting in May this year and again in August was that already several artists and previous residents had relocated to the area, an artist village in the making. A handful of other houses for residents are near completion, while one smaller hut recently finished holds a kitchen designed to host artists and creatives focusing on food. A correlated strand of the residency, Commons/Kuwa, launched in August, with Shizuoka-based artist Takayuki Watanabe devising a series of events over a week, including mochimaking. Sitting in Hamana’s house, among half-finished pots on the floor, overlooking a rice field waiting to be harvested the following week, we spoke about nostalgia, beauty and the end of capitalism.

ArtReview Asia Where did the idea for the residency and countryside community start for you?

Kazunori Hamana My uncle married a farmer’s daughter, and we went to her house when I was three. We still have the photo, it was 1973. We came into a house with a high grass roof and carved wooden beams, I was so shocked. I couldn’t speak, but I thought ‘What is this? What is this beauty, compared to my house?’ At six years old, I told my mother I wanted to build a house like that. And she said, ‘What? You crazy?’ My grandfather was a carpenter and I asked him if we could make a chicken coop. So we built a house together, and he bought a baby chicken too. I was so satisfied, going around outside with the chicken. I was a crazy kid. So I had always the idea of a rural life. Not so much as a farmer as occupation, but a handcrafted life, with nature. It wasn’t taught, my father or mother never told me. It was an intuition.

ARA When did that idea of rural life start to meet with the conception of a creative community?

KH Community came much later. First, it’s an individual question, a presence with nature. I was sick of living in the city. I escaped from my family when I was fifteen years old to a rural area, I stayed with a couple of farmers and went to agriculture school. Then I learned, with the other students, a different kind of sharing and relationship, a new kind of community or family. It wasn’t by design; accidentally, I was with other people in the middle of nature, I could go fishing, skateboarding, cycling and study. It let me come back to myself. Since then I continue to make sure I connect with nature and our ancestors’ handmade culture.

ARA Sounds idyllic, though these ancestors don’t just seem to be Japanese farmers for you; you worked with vintage clothing for a period, and in other interviews you’ve spoken about your appreciation for denim as an ‘American mingei’ or folkcraft in itself. How are these things related for you?

KH In the late 1970s or early 80s I would go shopping with my mother, but I didn’t like anything she chose. Every garment. I hated it all. At that time, it was all nylon and polyester in Japan. Then, when I was eleven years old, I found Converse, canvas shoes made in the USA. It was totally different, better quality. I found Levi’s 501: work clothes, well-crafted, thick material, 100 percent cotton. We didn’t have that kind of clothing here. So I started going to clothes shops by myself, and I started collecting T-shirts and sweatshirts like the Champion reverse-weave. Eighties Japan was terrible. Everything my mother chose was classic of the time, but plastic. The new thing was better. Handcrafting had been forgotten; an aesthetic and an aesthetic intuition had been lost. How can I explain it? We see the ocean, or sunlight, and we think it’s beautiful: this is aesthetic intuition. This kind of aesthetic I found in Levi’s 501s.

ARA Levi’s also based its brand on a rugged cowboy image, and a sort of idealised vision of American countryside. What role does nostalgia play in this return to a rural lifestyle?

KH About every 30 years, we feel nostalgia for a past time. Vintage is a big trend now, but it’s also looking for more story and craftsmanship apart from the mass production of Uniqlo or Zara. It’s not a return to the past, but about looking for a better balance. Of course, I use a smartphone and drive a car. The reality is we are losing physical relationships and the connection to nature. Everything is too industrial; industry is, of course, important, but not too much. It’s the same with capitalism: we need it, but its purpose is just about making more money than other people; about trying to be famous; and just to consume, consume, consume. But that’s not a true purpose, because you’re never satisfied. It’s just like, what’s new? Look at Netflix, TikTok. There are a thousand times more movies today, but they all look the same. We have to hurry, we have to watch more. People get bored anyway in one second, so why spend the time making something better? I don’t think that before the 1950s, or during the nineteenth century, or under feudal society everything was perfect, or everyone back then was a genius, but you had to spend more time and e²ort making something. People were more sensitive because they weren’t as addicted to consumption. For me, it’s all connected, because my purpose is to try to find beauty every day; there is satisfaction in that. Now I collect abandoned houses. But the old farmhouses are similar to 501s. To work hard, you need tough clothes. A house is the same, you know? Handcrafted materials, built physically to be better. You have to cut wood, and do it all analogue. Building up old-style houses each day is an opportunity to try to be better: that’s art for me.

ARA While that work and your farming is situated in the Chiba landscape, your ceramics are exhibited in New York, London, Los Angeles. What is that kind of art for you?

KH For me art is creating. So of course I’m doing exhibitions, art fairs, but it’s not the main purpose for me. It’s nice to share time with the audience and sometimes someone buys something. That’s a wonderful thing, but it’s not my priority. I like making things; someone else might think my creation is art and want to share the piece.

ARA So it’s their choice if they see it as art. How did you come to making ceramics?

KH People appreciate my work like a sculpture, but I would say it’s more a result of my activity of fixing houses, making communities, my respect for handcrafted methods. The pots are not art, they are a leftover from those activities. Twenty-eight years ago I started living in front of the ocean, both to be able to ignore the business mindset and for my own happiness. I started catching fish, I spent three months making a fishing net, for my own satisfaction and intuition. Making the pots was the same, I wanted to make a natural thing. It was a lot of fun and joy. I didn’t have a plan; I was not going to sell them. Later I started growing rice, and the rice is not for sale. It’s similar. As a result of making, some people started buying the ceramics, and I invest that money into the houses. But exhibitions, the market, that’s not my purpose; my main purpose is the day-to-day of challenging myself.

ARA The question of circulation comes to mind; the ceramics circulating enable the community here to circulate, and they kind of orbit each other in a certain way. But usually, for an art career, it’s about awareness of a practice or maker in the first place. There’s lots of self-taught artists who never sell anything, and it’s one thing working here, farming rice and making pots, and then also being featured in The New York Times or Vogue Japan , as you have been. How did the ceramics begin to circulate in that way?

KH I did the ceramics for a long time before I showed people. I first shared these online, on Tumblr in the 2010s, shooting the ceramics on my camera at the beach house in front of the ocean. It was very wild and seemed to touch a subconscious demand in people; the wood, the clay, the basic thing of touching mud.

ARA So it began as an image distributed online?

KH It wasn’t an art context, and clay wasn’t at that point as popular in art: handcrafts weren’t really seen as high art. Many followers started on Tumblr, mostly from New York at the time. Conversations with artists started on DMs, like Takayuki Watanabe, who is doing an event in the kitchen here, and Takashi Murakami, who wanted to show a new Japanese craft movement to a us audience. So it ended up in an art context.

ARA How important is the wild countryside context in the white-walled gallery where these pieces end up sometimes?

KH I made it in context, with the ocean and nature. It’s a remaining trace, the context is carried within the object. Some people have said to me that they see what I’m doing, making rice, building community, as an ideal thing for humans to do. And they feel that, but they cannot do it themselves, so they see my work as omamori – a good luck charm.

ARA How do you feel about being a good luck charm? Is there a sense of performing a kind of ideal countryside for city dwellers?

KH Maybe it’s true. Maybe that’s why people appreciate my life and my work, but that’s also a kind of result. I can’t save people, but I can be an alternative example. Things are also changing; over a decade ago, I started talking about community building and fixing. In the artworld here, the emphasis then was on the concept in an artwork, the art-history context, and the artist producing painting, sculptures, artworks where the idea is in the physical piece. Talking about Commons/Oppes, people told me, “You cannot be an artist if you keep doing this. Why go the long way?” They didn’t understand my goal; they thought I was lazy, wasting opportunities. But I didn’t follow this system. I was spending time making rice, trying to build a new type of community. The art market is just a market. My life as an artist is not focusing on the market or sculpture; it’s challenging everything to be better, to find more beautiful things. This challenge is art. After ten years I’ve done a lot of things I planned for a long time, and now they see. And how people are talking about art is changing, especially after the pandemic. Before it was concept and object, now it’s… how can I explain it? I cannot explain. It’s vibes.

ARA Within that daily process and challenge, where the ceramics are a byproduct, why is it this form of a large vase particularly that you keep returning to?

KH I tried many shapes and, of course, I still want to try different shapes. In Japan you often see the tsubo shape, often smaller, practical vases for seeds or food storage. But at a local museum decades ago I saw an old pot with a beautiful organic line to it, and it was a striking size. I found out it was a funeral pot for children, made to fit the body of the child. I felt something close to the mind of the parents. So for now I’m making this; I don’t know about next year. But this shape is a kind of symbol of a parent’s, a human’s love.

ARA There’s a living-museum aspect to what you’re doing: actively trying out ways of living to see what happens, drawing on the past but mixed in with aspects of the present. In terms of the structures you’re fixing up, it’s not all old farmhouses but a range of eras, older and more recent. Most of the older architecture preserved in Japan is castles and homes of the wealthier parts of society, creating a certain vision of the past. What do you feel you’re building here?

KH I’m trying to rewrite the nostalgia, so it’s not just a rich-person aesthetic. We made a mess from the 1970s to today, the buildings were very ugly, all plastic inside. Now, people just demolish, demolish, demolish. But demolishing 1970s buildings is not the answer. It’s easy to demolish and build. But if you keep building new, do you really have an aesthetic? We have to understand why we are lost. What kind of mistakes did we make? And what shouldn’t we do?

ARA Also, whose aesthetic? I mean, yes, most humans can agree a sunset is beautiful. But then with architecture, or art, it gets a little bit more difficult.

KH The most important thing to me is a connection with nature. I’m not just keeping ugly houses, I’m arranging parts of them to make sure we can connect again to what’s outside and around us. Then if we understand what we should arrange, we learn; then if I design a new house, I can do it better. Staying here working like this, I’m learning every day. We’re building a new type of village, an open village.

ARA It seems to be about reconnecting production and exchange to a locality; smaller circuits of circulation that then can work strategically within larger circuits of circulation, not being everywhere all the time.

KH I think some people now realise convenience and speed are a waste of time. Happiness is making your own world, your own creation, and sharing it with a few people. Some people. Not with everyone. We have to find a balance of size, of cost, of nature. How can you be an artist if your rent is $3,000 a month? You cannot be creative with worry. You have to be free, and you need space. So it could be coming to Chiba for three months, where it accidentally remained old-school countryside and the rent is much lower. Or it could be somewhere like Idaho, or in France. Connect with nature, then you can more easily create something. This is my philosophy. I think for the twenty-first century we need this kind of community. Everybody has to be an artist and challenge oneself. Because it’s already started, you know; we share space, food. It’s a good point now, many people are sick of capitalism. Of course, still, maybe until I die, I will use money. But I try to count on money less and less. I’m lucky to get money from my ceramics; but maybe soon, if people are more artistic, no one will want to buy: we can just share and empathise in making. Our destination is in good vibes, good emotion. This is the future goal, a challenge for the next thousand years. That’s why we should think about global warming and being sustainable. Because for the future – of course we will be dead – but we want our kids and future humans to be happy, we have vibes connected to the future and the past. I want this planet to be beautiful, not just for humans, but animals and plants, for the next century and the next.

Kazunori Hamana is a visiting collaborator in Matthew LutzKinoy’s exhibition The Mud Room at Amant, New York, 17 September – 29 November , and his solo exhibition is at Saatchi Yates, London, from 19 November

グッチ（GUCCI）が、2027年クルーズコレクション「GucciCore」の広告キャンペーンを発表した。撮影を手がけたのは、都市空間における人間の営みを独自の視点で捉えてきた写真家、ピーター・フンク（Peter Funch）。ニューヨークを舞台に、都市と人々の関係性を描き出す。

キャンペーンを構成するのは、ニューヨークの街を行き交うさまざまな人々の姿を捉えた一連の写真だ。都市における個人と集団の関係を長年探究してきたフンクは、異なる個性やファッションが交差する瞬間に目を向け、一人ひとりの存在感と、群衆の中に生まれるつながりを浮かび上がらせる。

「GucciCore」は、2026年5月にニューヨークのタイムズスクエアで開催されたランウェイショーで初披露されたコレクション。グッチのスタイルの基盤となるワードローブをテーマに、ピーコートやトレンチコート、ビジネススーツ、シャツ、ペンシルスカートなどの定番アイテムを展開する。実用性と着やすさを重視しながら、イタリアらしい華やかさとエレガンスを融合させた。

街を行き交う人々の個性と、都市が生み出す集合的な風景。フンクの写真を通して、ファッションとストリート、個人と群衆の関係を映し出すキャンペーンとなっている。

Lee reappears as another female elder in “The King’s Fuxi,” which jumps ahead by at least one millennium — people no longer have tails, and their diet has diversified. article_text:
Lauded for the stylized studio environments of his debut fiction feature, 2021’s Locarno prizewinner “A New Old Play,” Qiu Jiongjiong returns to the soundstage for a second helping in his follow-up, “ Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting .” “A New Old Play” told the story of an actor who played different roles in successive epochs of Chinese history, and made his life into a three-hour pageant by using stage techniques: rippling bedsheets dyed a watery blue for ocean waves; fake plastic trees for nature. “Fuxi” has no such neat thematic relation between subject and style, but it’s a joy to be back on the soundstage with Qiu regardless.

Now acting as his own production designer as well, writer-director-editor Qiu serves up more painted backdrops and practical theatrical effects, this time in an anthology film in which a cast toplined by Lee Kang-sheng play multiple roles in rhyming chapters centered around food. It’s a four-course feast for the eyes, even if “A New Old Play’s” intertwined themes of art, memory, and China’s tumultuous 20th century offered more food for thought.

“Fuxi” — a word translated by an opening title card as “a tasty delicacy, or the act of eating it” — circles ideas of ritual and community, embodied by tasty-looking Sichuan food and, at times, fairly detailed instructions for cooking it. The appeal to arthouse audiences is obvious, though the international critics and programmers who compared “A New Old Play” to Jia Zhangke’s politically ambitious “Platform” may find “Fuxi” less substantial. Qiu operates in a more folkloric mode, beginning with the film’s first segment, “The Ancestors’ Fuxi,” set among a prehistoric tribe whose members are recognizably human, except for their tails. As a member of the tribe approaches the end of her life, it is explained, she cuts off her own tail, and prepares it as a soup, to feed her descendants as part of her burial rites.

The dying granny, who chops away at her appendage with a prop hatchet, is played by Lee, sporting a silver wig seemingly fashioned of rope. Famous as Tsai Ming-liang’s longtime muse, Lee has a sly charisma that peeks out at the edges of even his most morose roles, as it does here. Lee reappears as another female elder in “The King’s Fuxi,” which jumps ahead by at least one millennium — people no longer have tails, and their diet has diversified. There’s agriculture now — villagers toil behind tiered hillsides fashioned from flat boards painted with abstract green swirls — and animal husbandry.

In the “Ancestors” segment, wild dogs, played by actors in masks and black unitards, howl on the village outskirts; by the second segment, they’re kept as pets, and one (voiced by Qiu himself) even narrates the story. Society has become more hierarchical: The food Lee’s character serves is an offering to her king, who has abdicated in order to live as a bird (he floats through hand-painted clouds and smoke-machine haze on digitally removed wires), but still returns once a year to taste the tribute of his subjects.

This king is based on Duyu, a figure from Sichuan legend (“Duyu” means “cuckoo”), and one who may be inspired by a real figure who introduced the core principles of farming to the region. But even as “Fuxi” moves into recorded history, it remains in a liminal space between textbook and myth, material world and spirit world. In the third, most substantial segment, “The Litterateur’s Fuxi,” four spirits — including one played by Xue Xuchun, who portrayed a similar underworld guide in “A New Old Play” — assemble in a 1997 represented by cutouts of skyscrapers backlit through lighting-gel windows. They’re gathering to share a festive banquet at which each course triggers a memory from the life of the Song dynasty dissident poet Su Dongpo (Lee Hong-chi); amid the artifice of Qiu’s mise-en-scène, overhead shots of pork belly browning on a bubbling skillet, or fish steaming in chilis, stand out for their earthiness, and the use of offcuts such as a lamb’s spine makes a stark commentary on the pains of exile.

If “Fuxi” has a political agenda, it’s to be found in this section’s look at the responsibilities of an artist, though the fourth section, “Sworn Brothers’ Fuxi,” set at the dawn of the 20th century, is much more typical in its oblique and disguised musings on the promises and disappointments of modernity. A boy (Zhou Jiarui, one of the great-grandsons in “The Ancestors’ Fuxi”) runs away from servitude in a kitchen and, pursued by officers of the dying Qing dynasty, falls in with three of the spirits from the previous chapter, a motley gang of outlaws or ghosts who teach him to make congee, and about the virtues it requires — patience when preparing a meal, camaraderie when sharing it. The film’s overarching philosophy, as summed up in its final sequences, is stoic, bawdy and not particularly deep: “We eat, we shit, and that’s it, as of old.”

Freedom, for Qiu, seems to mean the freedom, in his storytelling, to repeatedly cross borders between life and death, and between different layers of fiction. “Fuxi” has a frame story, but it’s hard to tell where the frame ends and the story begins: Sol (Wen Ke) and Luna (Xiao Luxi), wearing respective sun and moon headpieces, look down on the feasting mortals, occasionally falling to earth but also appearing in interstitial sequences tinted, like a silent movie, either sepia or steel-blue, in which a film crew preps the Fuxi sequences.

In a recurring image, Sol and Luna seesaw on a foam mountain, rising and falling in turn as the days and centuries flow by below. Qiu’s eloquence lies in such playful gestures, which are pleasurable for their own sake. “Fuxi” takes place on sets with the heightened artificiality of a Hollywood backlot; Qiu’s handcraft is so sumptuous and elaborate that “resourceful” doesn’t cover it. In an era when digital effects work — and, increasingly, gen-AI imagery — is used as a quick fix for corner-cutting productions at all budget levels, every one of “Fuxi’s” intricately wrought tactile flourishes is a luxury good.

The Coen brothers could be heading back to their hometown in Minneapolis for a reunion movie eight years after their last joint film, “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.”

While at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival , where they received a career tribute, Joel and Ethan Coen revealed they have several projects in the pipeline set in Minneapolis, where they previously shot “Fargo” in 1996 and “A Serious Man” in 2009.

Related Stories

Isabelle Huppert Says AI Hasn’t Replaced Her Yet: ‘It Really Is Me Acting’

Cannes Queer Animated Comedy ‘Jim Queen’ Scores New Sales at Busan (EXCLUSIVE)

“We haven’t discussed it in terms of plot or narrative or what kind of movie. But we’ve discussed going back because there are certain crew people we missed,” said Ethan, sitting alongside Joel, Lumiere festival chief Thierry Fremaux (who also heads Cannes), and film journalist Didier Allouche.

Popular on Variety

“Yes, there are a couple of other stories that we’ve thought about that would take place in Minneapolis, which is where we come from. So we’ll see if they haven’t sort of germinated to the point where we would go, you know, that’s what we’re going to do next, or we’re even going to definitely do,” said Joel Coen.

Joel was responding to a challenge from Oscar-winning actor Frances McDormand, his wife of 42 years, who had playfully urged them on stage at the Lumiere ceremony to complete the unofficial trilogy that began with “Fargo” and “A Serious Man.” “I think Fran wants to see it. We’ll see if we can accommodate her,” Joel joked.

Since Netflix’s “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs,” Joel went on to direct “The Tragedy of Macbeth,” starring McDormand and Denzel Washington, while Ethan made “Drive-Away Dolls” and “Honey Don’t!,” both co-written with his wife and longtime collaborator Tricia Cooke.

But the brothers said they have continued writing together and have several unproduced scripts. “We’ve written a lot of scripts that we’ve never made,” Ethan said. Joel then joked that “one of which we could not find on the computer.”

“One of the Minneapolis stories we were talking about had a main part intended for an actor who has since died. So we’re thinking, well, we’re not sure that’s going to work. That’s a consequence of aging,” Ethan said.

They also wrote a new script together while each was working on a separate film, but it now feels outdated to them. “It deals with issues in the culture that we’ve sort of moved on from, or the culture has moved on from. It feels more like a period movie now. Should we make it or shouldn’t we?” he said. “Ethan suggested they could simply introduce the film with a title card reading, ‘Sometime during the Obama administration.’ It’s almost now, but it’s not now anymore.”

Yet, the brothers aren’t looking to get overly political, even if their films are often satires. “Things like the political situation in the United States are a kind of background against which you tell stories. But the idea of literalizing it in terms of Trump specifically is probably not in our wheelhouse, in terms of how we think about a story,” Joel said.

“We don’t really think of any of our movies as commenting on America currently, or commenting on anything outside the story itself. Audiences are entitled to take our movies any way they want. Making those comparisons may be totally appropriate for an audience, but we literally don’t think about it that way,” Ethan said.

The Coens also weighed in on the changing film business, including the role of streaming platforms, which have backed some of their recent projects. Netflix produced and released “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs,” while Joel’s “The Tragedy of Macbeth” was released theatrically by A24 before streaming on Apple TV+.

Asked about the impact of streaming on cinema, the brothers said they had mixed feelings, pointing out that their own careers had benefited from the rise of home video in the 1980s, when studios were more willing to finance independent films because they had additional ways of making money.

“In a strange way, we owe our careers to the fact that there were other formats for distribution, and they happened to be home video formats,” Joel said, adding that it would be “disingenuous” for them to oppose new distribution platforms outright.

But Joel also defended the theatrical experience, echoing his comments during the masterclass he took part with Ethan in Lyon on Friday. The worst thing you can get is somebody saying, ‘I loved your movie. I saw it on an airplane.’ It’s very discouraging,” Joel said. “This festival is all about sitting in a big room with a lot of people in the dark watching it. There’s no substitute for that. And so every filmmaker, I think, feels that way.”

He argued streamers themselves are starting to recognize the importance of theatrical releases again. “I actually think there’s a point now in which the streaming services are recognizing again the value of theatrical distribution, and my hope is that that will continue and everyone will see it as a net advantage,” Joel noted.

Asked about AI, Joel dismissed the idea that AI could take over screenwriting as “nonsense,’ but was critical of the “computer-generated images” that AI is helping create, even if helps filmmakers creating images and worlds that would otherwise be impossible.

“In a way, everything’s becoming a cartoon. Every movie is an animated movie, or it’s becoming more and more like that, especially because of things like AI and effects that are done in a computer,” he said.

Joel cited their 1990 film “Miller’s Crossing,” recalling how the opening shot of a hat blowing through the woods was created using thin wires manipulated by crew members outside the frame.

“There’s no one on earth that would do it that way now. It would be animated, and I’m quite certain that it would not be as beautiful. You do lose certain things with certain kinds of visual effects, and you would certainly lose them with AI,” he continued.

The brothers were also quizzed about the impact of the Paramount–Warner Bros. merger on filmmakers.

“The honest answer is I really don’t know how that’s all going to shake out. And I don’t know enough about the politics between who’s owning what,” Joel said, laughing nervously when he was pressed about the merger. “I do know that, obviously, the more all these companies are consolidated into one or two companies, or three companies, that’s not good. Because competition is what drives the market, but it’s also what produces opportunities for different kinds of movies.” On Paramount leadership, specifically, he said, “I don’t know about David Ellison.”

article_text:
While I enjoyed your photo feature with its “groundbreaking images [that] have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power” ( Muscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad), 17 October ), I felt that a more fitting sporting example than Gazza’s tears would have been Alex “Hurricane” Higgins at the 1982 World Snooker Championship.

On winning the title, Higgins, a notoriously erratic and divisive figure, broke down in tears and pleaded for his wife and infant daughter to join him. It was not an act of image management, popularity-seeking or virtue- signalling. Rather, it was the spontaneous reaction of a man who simply wanted to share the greatest moment of his career with his young daughter.

The scene was made all the more poignant by what followed. With the benefit of hindsight, and in light of Higgins’s subsequent decline into sporting wilderness and personal hardship, that moment stands as a fleeting glimpse of unguarded joy and human vulnerability. In that respect, it remains one of sport’s most moving displays of emotion.

And if Alex Higgins , a man renowned for his toughness, volatility and refusal to conform, could openly weep in public and clutch his baby daughter at the pinnacle of his career, perhaps it serves as a reminder that showing emotion diminishes neither the man nor the achievement. Paul Mitchell Belfast

article_text:
It has been a summer of change for Pace Gallery , and its 2024 accounts that were filed 10 months late with Companies House, the British government’s business register, reflect that.

The group’s turnover totaled $67.69 million in 2024, a 35.5 percent drop from 2023, which cashed in $104.95 million. A pre-tax loss of $2,429 was recorded for 2024 compared to a $6.8 million profit for 2023. (The mega-gallery’s UK registered company, The Pace Gallery Limited, serves as the umbrella company for its operations in Europe and Asia, excluding Tokyo as well as the US.)

“This reflected a continuation of the sector-wide contraction in global and UK art markets as well as a continued reluctance by some clients to buy which became most pronounced in 2024 and continued through 2025 and into 2026,” Pace Gallery said in the filing. “The market conditions led the directors to initiate cost saving measures across the group, but despite these measures, difficult market conditions continued.”

Net assets totaled $2.48 million compared to $4.51 million for 2023, while $9.39 million was payable to its US parent company, The Pace Gallery LLC, which in 2023 was $17.31 million. Further numbers show that The Pace Gallery Limited’s debt of $19.2 million will be turned into shares by the end of 2026 as it’s unable to repay $19.2 million to its US parent company.

“The proposed debt-for-equity conversion is part of a broader global financial management strategy, which reflects a capital structure decision within the Pace group and should not be interpreted as a loss or a liquidity issue for the UK business,” a Pace spokesperson said. “As part of the ongoing management of our global operations, we periodically review how our subsidiaries are financed to ensure that their balance sheets appropriately reflect the long-term nature of the capital invested in those businesses.”

The gallery added that the parent company has determined that a portion of its investment in the UK operation is more “appropriately reflected as equity rather than intercompany debt. The proposed transaction is intended to strengthen the UK company’s balance sheet and align its capital structure with the long-term needs of the business.”

Back in June, Pace’s London property was put on the market , with the gallery saying it was seeking a “less corporate” space in the British capital. Last month, Pace announced it was seeking tenants for part of its Chelsea headquarters.

Pace CEO Marc Glimcher recently told reporter Julie Brener Davich in the Substack The Appraisal that by early 2026, the company was convinced that “we needed to make real change in the structure of the business to adapt to the new reality.” He explains that this new reality takes into account factors such as: rising interest rates, global instability, the closing of the 1031 exchange tax loophole, as well as managing logistics costs for shipping and crating.

article_text:
It’s late January, and the intrepid Film Comment crew is on the ground reporting from an extra special edition of the Sundance Film Festival—the last to take place on the snowy slopes of Park City, Utah, the festival’s home since 1981, before moving to Boulder, Colorado in 2027. For the next week, we’ll be gathering the best critics on the scene to talk about each day’s premieres on the Podcast.

For our third Podcast from the fest, Film Comment Editor Devika Girish invited critics and FC Podcast veterans Tim Grierson, Robert Daniels, and Monica Castillo to discuss some of this year’s buzziest premieres to date, including Cathy Yan’s art world–satire The Gallerist (3:00), Gregg Araki’s erotic romp I Want Your Sex (20:15), and Olivia Wilde’s couples’ night dramedy The Invite (31:45, 42:40).
excerpt_original: Readymades: Tim Grierson, Robert Daniels, and Monica Castillo join to discuss The Gallerist , I Want Your Sex , and The Invite

article_text:
Paris Photo and Aperture are pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards—an annual celebration of the photobook’s enduring role within the narrative of photography. Now in its fourteenth year, the awards recognize excellence in three major categories of photobook publishing: First PhotoBook, PhotoBook of the Year, and Photography Catalog of the Year.

This year, Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards received a record number of books from fifty-six countries around the world, including standout entries from Armenia, Iran, Morocco, Venezuela, and more. On September 22–24, the 2026 shortlist jury met in New York for three concentrated days of review and deliberation by an international team: Alejandro Cartagena , artist; Alexandra Cunningham Cameron , director of design, Judd Foundation; Michael Famighetti , editor in chief, Aperture; Anna Planas , artistic director, Paris Photo; and Anshika Varma , curator and founder, Offset Projects.

“Reviewing the many submissions from around the globe underscores how photography books are a quietly powerful medium with endless possibilities for design, storytelling, and reflection on human experience,” says Michael Famighetti. Anna Planas adds, “The jury brings together different perspectives on photography and publishing. Through the selection presented at Paris Photo, we aim to highlight the photobook as a space for experimentation and to celebrate its importance within photography today.”

The shortlisted books will be exhibited at Paris Photo, open to the public from November 11 through November 15, followed by an international tour, including in Dublin at PhotoIreland, December 2026, and other venues to be announced.

On Thursday, November 12, a ﬁnal jury composed of ﬁve members will meet in Paris to select the winners for all three prizes, which will be revealed on Friday, November 13, at 3:00 p.m. (CET), at a ceremony at Paris Photo, and announced on Aperture.org and Parisphoto.com.

Below, see the thirty-five selected titles for the 2026 PhotoBook Awards shortlist.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 摄影师久井唯花的作品展“QUALIA”于2026年9月4日至17日在东京·银座的索尼影像画廊举办。久井以伴随色彩感觉的共感觉经验为背景，一直通过摄影记录视觉与非视觉感官相互联结的记忆。本次展览介绍与2025年出版的同名摄影集相呼应的作品世界。

article_text:
写真家・久井唯花の作品展「QUALIA」が、2026年9月4日から17日まで、東京・銀座のソニーイメージングギャリーで開催されている。色感覚を伴う共感覚の経験を背景に、視覚と非視覚的な感覚が結びついた記憶を写真によって記録してきた久井。2025年に刊行した同名写真集にもつながる作品世界を紹介する。

久井が制作の主題としているのは、人それぞれに異なる「知覚」のあり方だ。大阪芸術大学大学院で写真を学び、自身の共感覚の経験を起点に、目に見えるものだけでは捉えきれない感覚や記憶を写真へと置き換えてきた。2025年には、10年にわたって撮影した記録を写真集『QUALIA』としてまとめている。

タイトルの「QUALIA（クオリア）」は、あるものを見たり、聞いたり、感じたりした際に生じる、個人に固有の感覚的な質を指す言葉。本展に寄せたステートメントで久井は、「わたしの祈りは叶わないまま輝いている」と記している。過ぎ去った時間や、他者とは共有することのできない感覚。それらがどのようなかたちで写真として定着したとしても、その「輝きは、失われることはない」と語る。

展示作品にも、そうした知覚の揺らぎを思わせる像が現れる。資料に掲載された作品では、光に溶け込むような人物や水面、魚、海へ伸ばされた手などが、鮮明な記録というよりも記憶の中の光景のように写し出されている。色彩のにじみやブレ、強い光によって被写体の輪郭が曖昧になり、見る者自身の感覚や記憶を呼び起こしていく。

写真は世界を客観的に記録する装置である一方、撮影者が何をどのように「見た」のかを残す、極めて主観的なメディアでもある。「QUALIA」はその性質を手がかりに、同じものを見ても同じようには感じることのできない、人間の知覚の個別性へと目を向ける展覧会だ。

translated_excerpt_zh: 摄影师久井由香的展览《QUALIA》将于2026年9月4日至17日在东京银座的索尼影像加里举办。基于伴随色彩感觉的联觉体验，我用照片捕捉连接视觉和非视觉感官的记忆。
